FINAL HYPOTHESIS (natural-language, deliverable):
Among black respondents in the NLSY-79 processed file, incarceration (ever_jailed = 1, jailed 1985–1994) is strongly associated with reduced wealth accumulation through 1996, and the penalty is expressed in two ways depending on baseline economic status. Because the file contains no income variable, "income levels" are operationalized — as an explicit assumption — as rank-based quartiles of baseline composite_wealth_1985 (an asset-based proxy). Within every baseline-wealth quartile, ever_jailed = 1 black respondents accumulated far less wealth between 1985 and 1996 than ever_jailed = 0 peers: mean Δ(1996−1985) gaps were −$19,003 in Q1, −$16,061 in Q2, −$41,742 in Q3, and −$58,317 in Q4 (pooled −$33,489). In absolute dollars the wealth penalty of incarceration is thus largest for high-baseline (Q3–Q4) black respondents — the top quartile's jailed group actually lost wealth on average (mean Δ = −$5,043) while non-jailed peers gained +$53,274. However, for low-baseline (Q1–Q2) respondents the comparison is uniformly at the floor: medians of composite_wealth_1996 are $0 for both jailed and non-jailed (median DiD ≈ 0, constrained by ties-at-zero), yet even there jailed means are only ~21–35% of non-jailed means and 57% of jailed respondents sit at exactly zero wealth in 1996 (vs 33% of non-jailed). Across all strata the jailed-to-non-jailed mean wealth ratio falls from ~0.34–0.86 in 1985 to ~0.19–0.35 by 1996. Robustness: the mean Δ96 jail penalty is negative for both black (−$33,489) and white respondents (−$92,678), so the direction of the penalty is not black-specific; the black-vs-white triple difference is positive (+$59,189) only because white jailed respondents started from much higher wealth. Sex-stratified male-only results (n=143 jailed vs 1,322 non-jailed) reproduce the pattern with even larger gaps (Q4 mean DiD −$76,192); the black jailed female cell (n=16; all medians $0) is reported but too small for separate inference. Interpretation: incarceration is associated with a broad wealth penalty for black individuals that is largest in absolute terms for those with higher pre-incarceration assets and manifests as persistent floor-level stagnation (medians pinned at zero) for those with lower assets. This is an observational association, not a causal effect: mechanical wealth suppression during 1985–1994 incarceration, baseline imbalance ($320 vs $764 median composite_wealth_1985 for jailed vs non-jailed black respondents), small jailed cells, absence of income/age/incarceration-timing variables, duplicate rows treated one-per-respondent, and ever_jailed being the only incarceration indicator (no residence field exists to identify detention facilities) all limit causal reading.

payload.hypothesis: Among black respondents (NLSY-79 processed file), incarceration (ever_jailed = 1, jailed 1985–1994) is associated with substantially lower wealth by 1996 at every economic-status level, where 'income levels' are proxied — as a stated assumption, since no income variable exists — by rank-based quartiles of baseline composite_wealth_1985. Within every baseline-wealth quartile, jailed black respondents gained far less wealth from 1985 to 1996 than non-jailed peers (mean jailed-minus-non-jailed gaps: −$19,003 in Q1, −$16,061 in Q2, −$41,742 in Q3, −$58,317 in Q4; pooled −$33,489), while at baseline the groups were nearly equal (gaps of roughly $0 to −$16,000). In absolute dollars the wealth penalty of incarceration is largest for high-baseline black respondents — the top-quartile jailed group's mean wealth actually fell (Δ = −$5,043) while non-jailed top-quartile peers gained +$53,274 (median DiD −$14,876) — whereas for low-baseline respondents the penalty manifests as floor-level stagnation: medians of composite_wealth_1996 are $0 for both groups (median DiD ≈ 0 due to ties at zero), yet jailed means remain only ~21–35% of non-jailed means and 57% of jailed respondents sit at exactly zero wealth in 1996 versus 33% of non-jailed. The jailed/non-jailed mean-wealth ratio falls from 0.34–0.86 in 1985 to 0.19–0.35 by 1996 in every quartile. Male-only results (n=143 jailed vs 1,322 non-jailed) show the same pattern with larger gaps (Q4 mean DiD −$76,192); the black jailed female cell (n=16, all wealth medians $0) is reported but too small for separate inference. A jail wealth penalty also appears for white respondents (mean Δ96 DiD −$92,678), so the direction is not black-specific; it is especially consequential for black respondents because jail incidence is far higher (159/3,013 ≈ 5.3%, vs 69/7,099 ≈ 1.0% for white). This is an observational association, not a causal effect: mechanical wealth suppression during 1985–1994 incarceration, baseline imbalance ($320 vs $764 median composite_wealth_1985), small jailed cells, absence of income/age/incarceration-timing fields, duplicate rows treated one-per-respondent, and ever_jailed being the only incarceration indicator (no residence field exists) all preclude a causal reading.
payload.workflow: 1) Profiled data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 rows; documented 6 columns; no missing values; 1,899 duplicate rows treated one-per-respondent; confirmed no income, age, or residence fields). 2) Restricted to race=='black' (n=3,013); built economic-status strata as rank-based quartiles of composite_wealth_1985 (deterministic random tie-breaking, seed 0); cell sizes by ever_jailed: 47/36/42/34 jailed vs 707/717/711/719 non-jailed. 3) Computed levels (median and mean of composite_wealth_1985/1990/1996) and changes d90 = 1990−1985, d96 = 1996−1985 by stratum × ever_jailed. 4) Built the DiD table (jailed Δ minus non-jailed Δ) for medians and means, pooled and male-only (female jailed n=16 flagged). 5) Triple-difference robustness using white (primary) and all-non-black (secondary) reference groups. 6) Verified floor effects (zero-wealth shares, jailed/non-jailed mean ratios). Executed script: analysis/nls_incarceration_analysis.py; console output preserved in analysis/output.txt.
